newsitem.title: USA: USDA chief urges House to keep tobacco insurance.
newsitem.headline: USDA chief urges House to keep tobacco insurance.

text.p: U.S. Agriculture Secretary Dan Glickman said Thursday that he opposes efforts to end federal crop insurance protection for tobacco growers.
Following a speech here, Glickman told reporters he has sent a letter to Congress registering his concerns.
House lawmakers are expected to vote on the issue sometime Thursday or Friday during debate on fiscal 1998 agriculture appropriations bill by mid- to late-afternoon Thursday.
The same amendment was defeated on a voice vote during committee work on the spending bill. However, the provision may stand a better chance on the House floor.
"There's some feeling some members want to put a marker down on tobacco," a House Republican aide said.

Last month, a group of state attorney generals reached a $368.5 billion settlement with tobacco companies. With that pact now facing an uncertain fate in Congress, many members want to demonstrate a tough stance on tobacco, the aide said.

However, opponents argue the measure would do nothing to curb smoking or injure tobacco companies. Instead, it would fall hardest on farmers who have invested heavily in tobacco production and often have few alternative crops.
Meanwhile, the agriculture spending bill pending in the House does contain $24.3 million to enforce Food and Drug Administration anti-teen smoking regulations.

That's less than the $34 million the Clinton administration requested. But earlier this week, the Senate Appropriations subcommittee on agriculture recommended no federal government funding for the initiative.
Panel Chairman Thad Cochran, a Mississippi Republican, said funding for the enforcement activities should come from the proposed tobacco settlement or from the states.
